name: Thyme

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: light, sandy, gritty, or rocky soil with sharp drainage
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Thyme likes light, sandy, gritty soil that drains fast.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: light loam or shallow rocky soil that drains freely
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Light loam or shallow rocky soil is fine, as long as it drains well.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: heavy or wet clay that stays soggy around the roots
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy or wet clay is a problem because it stays soggy around the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Thyme is a low Mediterranean sub-shrub that does best in poor, dry ground with little organic matter; rich, wet soil produces soft growth, weak flavor, and root rot. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed or mound for drainage rather than feeding the soil.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Thyme likes poor, dry, gritty soil and full sun. That sounds backward, but it comes from the dry Mediterranean, so rich, damp soil actually makes it weak and rot-prone and dulls the flavor. If your soil is heavy clay, plant thyme in a raised bed or mound so water drains away fast, and skip the compost.

ph.note_seasoned: Thyme grows well in neutral to slightly alkaline soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 8.0, and tolerates mildly acidic ground down to about 5.5. It is not fussy about pH as long as drainage is sharp; wet feet, not soil chemistry, is what limits it.
ph.note_beginner: Thyme is happy in soil that is neutral to a little bit chalky, about pH 6.0 to 8.0, and copes with slightly acidic soil too. It does not fuss over pH, so the main thing is to make sure the soil drains fast.

tip_seasoned: Treat thyme lean and dry: full sun, gritty fast-draining soil, infrequent water, and almost no feeding. Overwatering and rich soil are the top killers and the surest way to dull the flavor. Harvest often and shear the plant after it blooms; thyme goes woody with age, so plan to divide or replace it every few years.
tip_beginner: The trick with thyme is to not fuss over it. Give it the sunniest, driest, best-draining spot you have, water it only when the soil dries out, and do not feed it much. Snip it often and give it a light trim after it flowers. Thyme gets woody as it ages, so expect to replace or divide it every few years.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Thyme has very low fertility needs and is easy to over-feed. A little compost worked in at planting is plenty; established plants generally need no fertilizer at all. Over-fertilizing pushes soft, leafy growth at the expense of the concentrated oils that give thyme its flavor and aroma.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Thyme barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer actually works against it. A little compost mixed in when you plant is enough, and after that you can usually skip feeding entirely. Feed it heavily and you get lots of soft leaves with weaker flavor.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: N/A. Thyme is not fed by N-P-K targets; the goal is lean soil and minimal-to-no supplemental feed, so no fertilizer analysis applies.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: N/A. There is no fertilizer number to hit here, since the aim is to feed thyme as little as possible.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: At most a little compost worked in at planting; usually no feeding after that.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little compost at planting, and usually nothing after that.

companions.note_seasoned: Thyme pairs naturally with other sun-loving, low-water Mediterranean herbs that share its lean, sharply drained conditions, such as rosemary, sage, oregano, and lavender; group these together so one dry, waterwise bed suits them all. Thyme is also a traditional companion in the vegetable garden, where growers have long planted it near cabbage-family crops in the belief its aroma helps deter cabbage pests. Keep it away from thirsty, rich-soil plants whose watering would rot it.
companions.note_beginner: Plant thyme next to other plants that also like full sun and dry soil, such as rosemary, sage, oregano, and lavender. Many gardeners also tuck it near cabbage and its relatives, believing the scent helps keep pests away. Keep thyme away from plants that need a lot of water, because that wet soil will rot it.

good_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean herb with the same full-sun, lean-soil, low-water needs, so it shares a dry bed with thyme without forcing the wet conditions that rot it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rosemary and thyme are both drought-tolerant Mediterranean sub-shrubs wanting full sun and sharp drainage, so co-cultivating them lets one waterwise bed serve both and avoids the overwatering that rots thyme. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility, horticulturally well-supported but not a measured pest or yield effect.

good_seasoned.name: Sage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Another woody Mediterranean herb that thrives on the same lean, dry, sunny conditions, making it an easy dry-border companion for thyme.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Garden sage shares thyme's full-sun, well-drained, low-water requirements, so the pairing is sound co-cultivation in one dry bed. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility, not a measured effect.

good_seasoned.name: Oregano
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, spreading Mediterranean herb with matching lean-soil and low-water needs; it and thyme make a natural, drought-tolerant herb grouping.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Oregano is a low Mediterranean herb wanting the same full sun, sharp drainage, and lean water as thyme, so co-cultivation is straightforward. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility.

good_seasoned.name: Lavender
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean sub-shrub that wants the identical lean, dry, sharply drained conditions as thyme and draws the same pollinators; the two are classic dry-garden partners.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Lavender and thyme are both Mediterranean sub-shrubs demanding full sun, sharp drainage, and low water, and both are strong pollinator draws, so they co-cultivate well in a dry bed. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility plus pollinator benefit, not a measured effect.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage and other brassicas
good_seasoned.timing: plant nearby in the vegetable bed
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional companion pairing: growers have long set aromatic thyme near cabbage-family crops in the belief its scent helps discourage cabbage pests. Framed as tradition, not a measured effect, and the soil-moisture needs differ, so site thyme at the dry edge of the bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic herbs including thyme are a long-standing folk companion for the cabbage family, said to deter cabbage moths and worms. This is grower tradition rather than a documented trial, and brassicas want richer, moister soil than thyme, so the cultural match is loose; flagged at low confidence.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Likes the same sunny, dry spot as thyme.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same shared-conditions co-cultivation basis as the good_seasoned Rosemary entry. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Rosemary is a natural thyme partner because it asks for the same things: full sun, lean soil, and not much water. Grow them together and you can run one dry, waterwise bed rather than a watering compromise, which is exactly what keeps thyme from rotting at the roots. Both are woody Mediterranean herbs, so they age and look at home side by side.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Another sun-and-dry-soil herb that grows happily beside thyme.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Sage. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sage wants the same dry, sunny, well-drained conditions as thyme, so the two share a bed with no fuss. Keeping them together means you water the whole group sparingly, which is what thyme needs to stay healthy. Both are tough Mediterranean herbs that shrug off heat and drought once established.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Oregano
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Shares thyme's love of sun and dry soil.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Oregano. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Oregano is a low, spreading Mediterranean herb that likes the same lean, dry, sunny spot as thyme, so the two make an easy, drought-tolerant pairing. Group them and you can keep the watering light for both, which is the key to not rotting thyme. They also look good together as a low, fragrant herb patch.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lavender
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Loves the same dry, sunny conditions and brings in pollinators.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Lavender. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lavender and thyme are classic dry-garden partners: both come from the Mediterranean and want full sun, sharp drainage, and very little water, so one lean bed suits them both. Both also draw bees and other pollinators when they flower. Plant them together in free-draining ground and resist the urge to pamper either.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage and other brassicas
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A traditional pairing; many gardeners plant thyme near cabbage to help keep pests off.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same traditional folk-companion basis and soil-moisture caveat as the good_seasoned brassicas entry. traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Setting fragrant thyme near the cabbage family is an old companion-planting habit, the idea being that its strong scent helps confuse or deter cabbage moths and worms. Treat this as grower tradition rather than proven fact. One honest caveat: cabbages want richer, moister soil than thyme's lean and dry ideal, so plant thyme at the dry edge of the bed rather than in the heart of it.

bad_seasoned.name: Basil and other thirsty herbs
bad_seasoned.timing: keep in a separate, wetter bed
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Basil and similar moisture-loving herbs want steady water and richer soil, the opposite of thyme's lean, dry, sharply drained ideal. Grown together, the watering that keeps basil happy keeps thyme's roots too wet and invites rot, so give them separate conditions.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Basil is a tender annual needing consistent moisture and fertile soil, while thyme demands lean, dry, sharply drained conditions; the watering regimes are incompatible and the wetter one drives thyme toward root rot. mechanistic/medium: a clear cultural-conflict rationale, not a documented trial.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellowing on the tiny leaves and faint webbing on the stems, most likely in hot, dry weather or on stressed or crowded plants. Thyme is generally pest-resistant, so this is usually a minor, weather-driven problem.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny yellow speckles on the leaves and faint webbing on the stems, usually in hot, dry weather. Thyme rarely has pest trouble, so this is normally minor.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-feeding mites that flare in hot, dry conditions. Thyme has few pests overall and is typically grown with little or no pesticide.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small sap-sucking mites that show up in hot, dry spells. Thyme has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse plants with a strong spray of water, and use insecticidal soap if numbers climb. A hard harvest or shear removes much of the infested growth at once.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, and use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Cutting the plant back also removes most of them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun and good spacing for airflow and avoid drought-stressing container plants in heat. Vigorous, unstressed thyme rarely attracts mites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep thyme in full sun with room around it, and do not let potted plants bake bone-dry in a heat wave. Healthy plants rarely get mites.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional clusters of small soft-bodied insects on tender new growth, most likely on stressed or overcrowded plants. Rarely a serious problem on thyme.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, small soft bugs on new growth, usually only on plants that are stressed or crowded. Rarely a big deal on thyme.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find thyme. As with mites, thyme is fairly pest-resistant and seldom needs treatment.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes appear. Thyme has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers build. Improving airflow and removing stress usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. More air and less stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Full sun, lean soil, good spacing, and no overwatering keep thyme vigorous enough to shrug off aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep thyme in full sun with room around it, dry lean soil, and not too much water. Healthy plants rarely get aphids.

diseases.name: Root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed base at the soil line. It is the main way thyme is lost and is tied to wet, poorly drained soil rather than to cold.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves yellow and the plant wilts and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot at the base. This is the main thing that kills thyme, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne rots that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Waterlogged ground, not cold, is the underlying cause; thyme is intolerant of wet feet.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is wet soil, not cold weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus everything on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun, keep plants on the dry side, and never let thyme sit in wet ground. On clay or in humid regions, use a mound or raised bed and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in fast-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and never let thyme sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay or in humid areas, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Foliar fungal problems in humid weather
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Powdery-white coating, spotting, or grayish moldy patches on the foliage, favored by warm, humid, still air and on crowded or overhead-watered plants. A minor issue next to root and crown rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A powdery white film, spots, or grayish mold on the leaves in warm, humid weather, more likely on crowded plants. A minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi such as powdery mildew that are favored by humidity, crowding, and poor air movement. Thyme is fairly disease-resistant, so these are mainly a humid-climate and overcrowding issue.
diseases.cause_beginner: Leaf fungi like powdery mildew that like damp, still, humid air and crowded plants. Thyme is fairly disease-resistant, so this is mostly a humid-weather problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected foliage, open up airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. A hard harvest or post-bloom shear clears and renews the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off affected leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. Cutting it back also helps.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for air circulation, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and favor the taller, smooth-leaved culinary types over low woolly ones where humidity is high. Good airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. In humid areas, the upright leafy types handle it better than the low fuzzy ones.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. Water new plants until they are established, then let the soil dry between waterings; mature thyme needs little water and is quite drought-tolerant. Container plants dry faster and need checking, but should still dry out between drinks.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not often. Water a new plant until it settles in, then let the soil dry out before watering again. An established thyme needs very little water. Pots dry faster, so check them, but still let them dry between waterings.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to settle new plants while establishing; once mature, only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells. Keep plants on the dry side to avoid root rot.
watering.amount_beginner: A regular soak for a new plant, then much less once it is established.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings. Avoid wetting the foliage and crown, which invites rot in humid conditions.
watering.method_beginner: Pour water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, and let it dry out before watering again. Wet leaves and a soggy base are what make thyme rot.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting or dieback of whole shoots, and a plant that fails despite watering signal too-wet roots and likely root or crown rot, not drought. Flavor also weakens in soft, over-watered growth.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If leaves yellow and shoots wilt or die back even though you are watering, the problem is almost always too much water, not too little. Soggy roots rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Established thyme rarely shows true drought stress; light wilting in extreme heat that recovers overnight is normal and not a reason to increase watering.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Thyme almost never gets too little water once established. A little droop on a very hot afternoon that bounces back by morning is fine.

schedule_by_stage.rate: a regular soak to settle new plants
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The first season is the only time regular watering matters: water new thyme until it is established, then let the soil dry between waterings. Water at the base and keep the foliage and crown dry against rot in humid conditions.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water a new thyme regularly until it settles in, then let the soil dry out before watering again. Water at the base to keep the leaves and crown dry.

schedule_by_stage.rate: occasional deep watering in dry spells
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Mature thyme needs little water and is quite drought-tolerant: only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells, keeping it on the dry side to avoid root rot. The most common way to kill it is overwatering, and its flavor weakens in soft, over-watered growth. Container plants dry faster and need checking, but should still dry out between waterings.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Mature thyme needs very little water. Give it an occasional deep drink only in a long dry spell, keeping it on the dry side. Too much water rots it and weakens the flavor. Pots dry faster, so check them, but still let them dry between waterings.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through dormancy thyme wants next to no water; keep it on the dry side with sharp drainage and do not let the crown sit in wet winter soil.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter thyme needs almost no water. Keep it on the dry side and never let it sit in soggy soil.

watering.method_note_seasoned: The most common way to kill thyme is overwatering. When in doubt, water less.
watering.method_note_beginner: Remember: more thyme dies from too much water than too little.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters; taper off sharply once the plant is established.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water fairly regularly the first year while it gets established, then back off a lot.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Nursery transplants are already hardened; set them out after the last spring frost. Divisions and rooted cuttings should be hardened gradually before planting out.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you buy a plant from a nursery, you can put it straight in the ground after your last spring frost. There is no seed-starting step you must do.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Thyme is most reliably started from a nursery transplant, a division of an established clump, or a softwood cutting (cuttings root in about three to four weeks); it can be grown from seed, but the fine seed is slow and germination is uneven, so most gardeners skip it. Divide established plants in spring, and mixing the tiny seed with sand helps it spread evenly if you do direct-sow. To start seed indoors, scatter and barely cover the fine seed about 10 weeks before the last frost, and expect slow, uneven germination over two to three weeks.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easy, reliable way to grow thyme is to buy a small plant, divide an existing clump, or root a cutting. You can grow it from seed, but the seed is tiny and slow and does not come up evenly, so most gardeners buy a plant instead. If you do start from seed, scatter the fine seed and barely cover it, and start indoors about 10 weeks before your last frost, keeping it warm and moist until it sprouts.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering; thyme must never sit in standing water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A gritty, fast-draining potting mix, not a moisture-holding one.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in coarse sand or perlite so water runs straight through.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A coarse, free-draining potting medium; avoid peat-heavy moisture-retentive mixes.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Add coarse sand, perlite, or fine gravel to sharpen drainage.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check the soil, but still let it dry between waterings and never leave the pot standing in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container thyme needs only a very light feed, if any; do not over-fertilize.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In the coldest zones, or with a less hardy type, grow thyme in a pot you can move into an unheated but sheltered spot for winter, then bring it back out in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Where the chosen type is not reliably hardy, a container lets you overwinter the plant under cover (an unheated garage or porch); keep it on the dry side and protected from hard freezes, then return it outdoors after frost.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Thyme is one of the best herbs for containers: it likes to dry out between waterings, which a pot does readily. Use a wide, free-draining pot with a gritty mix, keep it in full sun, and never let it stand in water. A pot is also the easy way to overwinter thyme where winters are too cold for it in the ground.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Thyme does very well in a pot, partly because it likes the soil to dry out between waterings. Use a wide pot with holes in the bottom and a gritty mix, keep it in full sun, and tip out any water that collects in the saucer.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers keep the medium too consistently moist for thyme and promote root rot; use a conventional free-draining pot instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for thyme; they keep the soil too wet and the roots rot.

recommended.name: English (common) thyme
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9.
recommended.note: The standard broad-leaved culinary thyme, upright to about a foot tall; the all-purpose kitchen thyme.

recommended.name: French thyme
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy, similar to English thyme in roughly zones 5 to 9.
recommended.note: A narrow-leaved selection of common thyme with a slightly milder, sweeter flavor; a chef's favorite.

recommended.name: German Winter thyme
recommended.hardiness_note: Extra cold-hardy; the most reliable culinary type in cold-winter zones.
recommended.note: A robust, cold-hardy culinary selection with a strong classic thyme flavor; a good choice where winters are severe.

recommended.name: Lemon thyme
recommended.note: A citrus-scented culinary hybrid with green or gold-variegated leaves; excellent with fish and poultry.

recommended.name: Silver thyme
recommended.note: A silver-and-cream variegated selection grown as much for looks as for the kitchen; usable but chosen mostly for ornament.

recommended.name: Creeping thyme (mother-of-thyme)
recommended.hardiness_note: Very hardy, roughly zones 4 to 9; the hardiest common type.
recommended.note: A flat, mat-forming groundcover thyme grown between pavers and as a lawn substitute; ornamental more than culinary, though the foliage is aromatic.

varieties.note_seasoned: Thyme comes in several practical groups. Common or English thyme (Thymus vulgaris) is the standard broad-leaved culinary thyme, with French thyme a narrow-leaved, milder selection of the same species and German Winter a hardy, upright culinary selection. Lemon thyme (Thymus x citriodorus) adds a citrus note. Silver thyme is a variegated form grown as much for ornament. Creeping thyme (Thymus serpyllum, mother-of-thyme) is a flat, hardy groundcover used between pavers and as a lawn substitute, and is ornamental more than culinary. For the kitchen, start with English or French thyme; for a hardy groundcover, choose creeping thyme.
varieties.note_beginner: There are a few kinds of thyme. English (common) thyme is the all-purpose cooking thyme, and French thyme is a milder version of it. German Winter thyme is a hardy, upright type. Lemon thyme tastes citrusy and is great with fish. Silver thyme is a pretty variegated type. Creeping thyme is a flat, spreading groundcover you plant between stepping stones; it is grown more for looks than for cooking. For cooking, pick English or French thyme.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh cut sprigs hold for a few days in a glass of water on the counter. For long-term keeping, dry thyme: tie small bundles and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, airy place, then strip the leaves into a sealed jar out of the light.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Fresh sprigs last a few days standing in a little water on the counter. To keep thyme longer, dry it by hanging small bunches upside down somewhere warm and airy, then store the dried leaves in a sealed jar.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh sprigs loosely wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel in a bag, where they keep for one to two weeks.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep fresh thyme in the fridge, loosely wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel inside a bag, for one to two weeks.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole sprigs in a bag, or strip the leaves and freeze them in water or oil in ice-cube trays for cooking; frozen thyme keeps its flavor well for months.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze thyme: put whole sprigs in a bag, or freeze the leaves in water or oil in an ice-cube tray to drop into cooking later.
storage.notes_seasoned: Thyme is one of the sturdy herbs that dries easily. Cut stems for drying just before or as the plant begins to flower, when the oils are strongest, tie them in small loose bundles, and hang them in a warm, dry, airy spot; a paper bag around the bundle keeps off dust. Once dry, strip the leaves and store them sealed and out of the light.
storage.notes_beginner: Thyme is easy to dry. Cut stems just before it flowers, tie them in small loose bunches, and hang them upside down somewhere warm and airy (a paper bag around the bunch keeps the dust off). When dry, rub the leaves off into a sealed jar kept out of the light.

rotation.note_seasoned: N/A. Thyme is a perennial that stays in place for several years, so annual crop rotation does not apply. When replanting an old thyme patch, choose a fresh, well-drained site to avoid carrying over soilborne root rot.
rotation.note_beginner: N/A. Thyme is not rotated like a vegetable because it is a permanent plant that stays put for years. If you replace an old one, pick a fresh, well-draining spot.

growth_stages.name: Plant out
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Set the nursery plant, division, or rooted cutting out after the last spring frost, in the sunniest, sharpest-draining spot you have. Space plants 8 to 12 inches apart; on heavy ground, plant on a mound or raised bed.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After your last spring frost, plant the thyme in the sunniest, best-draining spot. Leave about 8 to 12 inches between plants so each has room and good airflow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A compact young plant with fine gray-green foliage and firm roots filling the pot, ready to set out once frost has passed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small, low bushy plant with tiny gray-green leaves and roots that hold the potting soil together when you slide it out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen the rootball, set the crown level with the soil surface, and water in once to settle the roots. Do not amend with rich compost or fertilizer; thyme wants lean ground.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Gently loosen the roots, plant so the top of the rootball is level with the soil, and water once to settle it. Skip the fertilizer and rich compost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Planted: type or cultivar, number set out, and the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down which thyme you planted and when.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year one)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first season after planting. Thyme grows slowly the first year while it builds roots, and reaches full size by about the second year. Harvest only lightly this season.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first growing season. Your thyme grows slowly while it builds roots and fills out by about year two. Only pick a little this year.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new growth low and outward as the plant begins to form a low, spreading mound. Light growth the first year is normal.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: New growth spreading low and wide as the plant fills in. Slow growth the first year is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water until the plant is settled, then taper toward infrequent watering. Harvest only lightly, and hold off on fertilizer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water fairly often until the plant takes hold, then water less. Only snip a little, and do not feed it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Establishment: planting-out date, watering taper, and any light harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you planted it and that you are watering less as it settles.

growth_stages.name: Spring leaf-out and harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Each spring the plant pushes fresh growth from the base and lower stems, and this leafy growth is what you harvest through the season by snipping sprigs as needed.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Every spring, new growth appears low on the plant. This leafy growth is what you snip through the season for cooking.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New soft growth emerging along the stems and crown, signaling the plant came through winter and is growing again.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Soft new growth low on the plant in spring. That tells you it survived winter and is growing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do any light shaping cut in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed. Begin harvesting sprigs as needed, and settle into infrequent watering as the soil warms.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In early spring, once you see new growth and frost is over, you can lightly trim it to keep it neat. Start snipping sprigs to cook with, and water deeply but not often.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Spring leaf-out: date growth resumed and any spring trim done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when spring growth started and if you trimmed.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The summer flowering window, when thyme puts up tiny lavender, pink, or white flower clusters that draw bees. Flavor is most concentrated just before and as the flowers open, so this is the best time to cut for drying.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Summer, when thyme makes tiny lavender, pink, or white flowers that bees love. The flavor is strongest just before and as it flowers, so this is the best time to cut thyme to dry.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small flower clusters coloring up on the stem tips. For the best flavor and dried quality, harvest as the first flowers begin to open.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Tiny flower clusters on the stem tips. For the best flavor, cut sprigs as the first flowers are just starting to open.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut sprigs for drying as the flowers begin to open. Keep watering light and do not feed; over-watering and rich soil weaken the flavor.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut thyme for drying as it starts to flower. Keep watering light and do not fertilize, since too much water or feeding dulls the flavor.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bloom: first-open date and any harvest cuts taken for drying.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it bloomed and when you cut thyme to dry.

growth_stages.name: Shear back
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The post-bloom shear, the key upkeep act of the year. After flowering fades, clip the plant back to remove the spent flower stems and tidy the mound, cutting into leafy growth and staying above the bare woody base.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The tidy-up trim after the flowers fade. Clip off the spent flower stems and shape the plant, cutting into the leafy growth and staying above the hard woody stems.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Spent, browning flower stems and a plant finished with its main bloom. Below the leafy growth you will see bare woody stems; those are your no-cut zone.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Faded, brownish flowers and a plant done blooming. Notice the woody stems below the green; do not cut into those.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Shear off the spent flowers and lightly reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth only, never into bare wood, which resprouts poorly. Regular harvesting plus this shear keeps thyme from going woody; even so, plan to divide or replace it every few years.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Trim off the old flowers and neaten the plant, cutting only into the leafy parts and not into the hard woody stems. Frequent snipping plus this trim keeps thyme bushy, but it still gets woody with age, so replace or divide it every few years.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Shear back: date sheared and roughly how much removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when you trimmed off the old flowers.

growth_stages.name: Dormancy (cold zones)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, thyme slows or goes semi-dormant. It needs almost no water, and it is wet soil, not the cold itself, that most often kills it over winter. Hardy types hold much of their foliage.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Where winters freeze, thyme mostly rests through the cold months. It barely needs water, and it is soggy soil, not the cold, that usually kills it over winter. The hardy types keep much of their leaves.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A plant that has slowed or stopped growing for the season. Hardy English and creeping types stay semi-evergreen; less hardy types decline in hard cold.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A plant that has slowed for the season. The hardy English and creeping kinds keep their leaves; less hardy types fade in hard cold.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop watering and feeding, and leave any hard shaping for spring. Protect less hardy types or move container plants under cover. In the coldest zones, good drainage and a sheltered spot help thyme overwinter.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering and feeding, and save any big trim for spring. Shelter the less hardy types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. In very cold areas, good drainage and a sheltered spot help thyme survive.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Dormancy: date growth slowed and any winter protection applied.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it went dormant and any winter cover you added.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your plant-out window is open. Set the nursery plant, division, or cutting in full sun in sharply drained soil after the last frost, spacing plants 8 to 12 inches apart. Skip rich compost and fertilizer.
notifications.body_beginner: It is time to plant your thyme. Put it in a sunny, well-draining spot now that frost has passed, leaving 8 to 12 inches between plants, and do not add fertilizer.

notifications.body_seasoned: Blooms are fading, time to shear off the spent flower stems and tidy the mound, staying above the woody base. Cut into leafy growth only. Regular harvest plus this shear slows the plant going woody.
notifications.body_beginner: Your thyme flowers are fading, so trim off the old flower stems and neaten the plant, cutting only into the leafy growth and staying above the hard woody stems. This keeps it bushy.

notifications.title_beginner: Get your thyme ready for winter
notifications.body_seasoned: Cold is coming. Stop watering and feeding, leave any hard shaping for spring, and protect less hardy types or move container plants under cover. Wet winter soil, not cold, is the usual killer.
notifications.body_beginner: Winter is coming. Stop watering and feeding, save any big trim for spring, and shelter the less hardy types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills thyme.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Late frost on tender new growth
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Late frost on the new growth
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A late spring frost is forecast while the plant is pushing tender new growth. Hold off on any planned shaping until frost has fully passed, and protect newly set-out plants overnight.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A late spring frost is coming while your thyme has soft new growth. Wait to do any trimming until frost is fully over, and cover any just-planted thyme overnight.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, humid weather raises rot risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A spell of humid heat is forecast, which raises the risk of root rot and foliar fungus in muggy regions. Do not add water on thyme's account, make sure it is not sitting wet, and keep airflow open around the plant.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, sticky weather is coming, which can lead to rot and leaf fungus. Do not give thyme extra water, make sure it is not sitting in wet soil, and keep the area around it open and airy.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Wet winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Soggy winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Prolonged wet soil is forecast heading into or during winter. Wet winter ground, not cold, is what most often kills thyme, so make sure it is not sitting in water and consider moving containers under cover.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A long wet spell is coming around winter. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills thyme, so make sure it is not standing in water, and move pots somewhere protected if you can.

transplant.text_seasoned: Plant thyme lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine, set it in the sunniest, sharpest-draining spot, and on clay build a mound or raised bed. Rich, wet soil weakens flavor and rots the roots.
transplant.text_beginner: Thyme does best in poor, dry soil, so do not add fertilizer or rich compost. Give it your sunniest spot, and if your soil is heavy clay, plant on a little mound or raised bed so water drains away.

transplant.text_seasoned: Space plants 8 to 12 inches apart for airflow. Good air movement between plants is one of the simplest ways to head off the foliar fungus thyme can get in damp or humid conditions.
transplant.text_beginner: Leave about 8 to 12 inches between plants. That space lets air move around each one, which helps prevent the leaf fungus thyme can get when it stays damp.

establishment.text_seasoned: Year one is about roots, not harvest. Water until the plant is settled, then taper toward infrequent. Harvest only lightly this season; thyme reaches full size by about the second year.
establishment.text_beginner: The first year is about growing roots. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water less. Only pick a little this year. Thyme fills out by about year two.

establishment.text_seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Thyme has low fertility needs, and over-fertilizing produces soft growth with weaker flavor. The same goes for water: more is not better.
establishment.text_beginner: Try not to feed it. Thyme needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives soft leaves with less flavor. The same is true for water, where more is not better.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Harvest little and often once the plant is established. Snipping sprigs regularly keeps thyme bushy and productive and slows it going woody; you can take leaves anytime for cooking.
vegetative.text_beginner: Once it is established, snip thyme often. Regular cutting keeps it bushy and slows it turning woody, and you can pick leaves anytime to cook with.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Do any shaping cut in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed. Cut into leafy growth, not the bare woody stems, which resprout poorly.
vegetative.text_beginner: If you want to tidy the plant, do it in early spring once new growth shows and frost is over. Cut only into the leafy parts, not the hard woody stems.

bloom.text_seasoned: For the strongest flavor, cut thyme for drying just before or as the first flowers open, when the leaf oils peak. Harvest in the morning once the dew has dried.
bloom.text_beginner: For the best flavor, cut thyme to dry just before or as it starts to flower, when the oils are strongest. Cut in the morning after the dew dries.

bloom.text_seasoned: Let some flowers open for the bees if you like; thyme blooms are a strong pollinator draw. To dry thyme, hang small bundles in a warm, airy place, then store the stripped leaves sealed.
bloom.text_beginner: You can leave some flowers for the bees, which love thyme blooms. To dry thyme, hang small bunches somewhere warm and airy, then store the leaves in a sealed jar.

cut_back.text_seasoned: Shear off the spent flower stems after bloom and lightly reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth and never into bare wood. Frequent harvest plus this shear keeps thyme compact, but it still goes woody with age, so divide or replace it every few years.
cut_back.text_beginner: After it flowers, trim off the old flower stems and neaten the plant, cutting only into the leafy parts, never the hard wood. Snipping often plus this trim keeps thyme bushy, but it still gets woody, so replace or divide it every few years.

cut_back.text_seasoned: Time the main shaping after flowering rather than in fall. A late-fall hard cut can leave the plant vulnerable going into winter, so save heavy shaping for after bloom or early spring.
cut_back.text_beginner: Do the main trim after it flowers, not in late fall. A hard trim just before winter can leave the plant weak, so wait until after bloom or early spring for heavy trimming.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Over winter, do almost nothing: stop watering and feeding, and leave hard shaping for spring. A plant in wet winter soil rots, so the worst thing you can do is keep it watered.
dormancy.text_beginner: In winter, do almost nothing. Stop watering and feeding, and save the trim for spring. Thyme sitting in wet winter soil rots, so do not keep watering it.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Protect the less hardy plants. English and creeping thymes are the hardiest and overwinter outdoors through the cold zones with sharp drainage and a sheltered spot; grow tender types or cold-edge plants in pots you can move under cover.
dormancy.text_beginner: Shelter the less hardy plants. English and creeping thyme are the toughest and can stay outside in cold areas if drainage is good and the spot is sheltered; grow tender types in pots you can bring under cover.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature plant yields a steady supply of sprigs through the growing season, easily enough to keep a kitchen stocked with fresh thyme plus bundles to dry; productivity is best once the plant reaches full size at about the second year.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown thyme plant gives you plenty of sprigs all season, enough to cook with fresh and to dry, especially once it is a couple of years old.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect only light harvests the first year; harvesting sparingly while the plant establishes pays off in fuller production from the second season on.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect much the first year. Picking lightly while the plant settles in gives you bigger harvests from year two.
factors_seasoned: Plant age and size (full production at about the second year)
Full sun and lean, sharply drained soil
Frequent harvesting to keep growth soft and non-woody
Type (upright culinary types yield more usable foliage than flat creeping ones)

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves turning yellow or the plant dying back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: With thyme, yellowing and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering and poor drainage are the number one killer, leading to root and crown rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: For thyme, yellow leaves and dieback usually mean too much water, not too little. Overwatering and soggy soil are the biggest killer. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back on watering hard and fix drainage. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on clay or in humid areas use a mound or raised bed. Never let thyme sit in wet ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on heavy or humid ground plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Woody and bare in the middle
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A thyme plant that has gone woody and bare or split open in the center is simply aging. Thyme goes woody with time even with good care; frequent harvest and a post-bloom shear slow it, but plants are best divided or replaced every few years.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When thyme gets woody and bare in the middle, it is mostly just getting old. All thyme goes woody eventually; snipping often and trimming after bloom slows it down, but plants are best replaced or divided every few years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Harvest regularly and shear after bloom to keep growth soft, cutting into leafy growth only, never into bare wood. Divide a healthy older clump or start a fresh plant from a cutting every few years to keep a vigorous supply.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Snip thyme often and trim it after it flowers, cutting only into the leafy parts. Every few years, split a healthy older plant or start a new one from a cutting so you always have a fresh, bushy plant.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Weak flavor or soft, floppy growth
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not much flavor or soft, floppy growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Bland thyme with soft, lush growth usually means too much feed, too much water, or too little sun. The concentrated oils that give thyme its flavor build up in lean, dry, sunny conditions and thin out in rich, wet, shady ones.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Thyme with little flavor and soft, floppy leaves usually has too much fertilizer or water, or too little sun. Thyme tastes strongest when it is grown lean, dry, and sunny.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Stop fertilizing, water less, and give the plant full sun. Lean, dry, sunny conditions concentrate the oils and give the strongest flavor; harvesting just before bloom captures the peak.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Stop feeding it, water less, and make sure it gets full sun. Poor, dry, sunny conditions give the best flavor, and picking just before it flowers captures the strongest taste.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: N/A. Thyme is a perennial planted once, not a crop sown in succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: N/A. You plant thyme once; you do not resow it through the season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Thyme is a woody perennial harvested continuously from the same plant over several years, so succession sowing does not apply; renew plants by division or cuttings every few years instead.

open_findings.summary: Regional planting/bloom windows are modeled from thyme phenology (early-to-mid-summer bloom: NCSU May-Jul, PSU Jun-Jul, UC Marin early summer) plus each zone's frost dates and the nearest readable T1 guidance, not from a thyme-specific per-region planting chart (no such chart was found for all 10 regions). Windows are generally-safe; tighten exact months at the variety-delta pass.

northern_tier zone 4 is modeled as a MARGINAL in-ground perennial (the hardiness refit vs lavender, which kept z4 annual). Common thyme is reliably hardy z5-9 (NCSU 5a-9b; PSU/UF/UMD z5-9); USU states thyme can be grown from zone 4 and creeping thyme is z4-9 (UF), so z4 is the hardy-type/sharp-drainage edge, not the reliable default. zone 3 kept annual/container. Confirm at review.

hawaii_tropical z11 is the lowest-confidence region: no CTAHR/T1 thyme page for Hawaii was found. Modeled as marginal, viable only in cool, dry upcountry microclimates and not the humid lowland (the same honest treatment lavender used for Hawaii), cited to general thyme culture rather than a Hawaii-specific chart. fl_peninsula z11 and se_gulf/humid cells are likewise marginal (root rot in humid heat, UF/IFAS). Community-correction invited.

The second disease entry leads with powdery mildew and general humid-weather foliar fungus (UF/IFAS names powdery mildew; UC Marin notes fungus in humid climates; PSU lists fungal diseases). Gray mold (Botrytis) is mentioned only as a general example of that humid-condition fungal class and is not pinned to a thyme-specific T1 statement; treat the gray-mold naming as modeled.

Companions are TRADITIONAL/low-to-medium confidence: shared-conditions Mediterranean-herb pairings (rosemary/sage/oregano/lavender) and the folk cabbage-family pairing (aromatic thyme said to deter cabbage pests), plus a mechanistic bad-pairing with thirsty herbs (basil) on the water-needs conflict. No thyme-specific companion trial was found in a readable T1 source; the cabbage-deterrent claim is framed as tradition, not measured effect.

Judgment calls: spacing [8,12] in (UMD/UMN 8-12 in; PSU/UC Marin ~12 in; NCSU 12 in to 3 ft); pH preferred [6.0,8.0] (NCSU/UF), tolerated down to 5.5 (WVU ~6.5, PSU 6.3); productive_lifespan_years [3,5] and establishment_years 2 (Aggie renew every 3-4 yr; UC Marin center dies out after a few years; USU ~5 yr / 90-day maturity; WVU full maturity 2nd year); germination_temp_f 70 (UC Marin soil 70F); hardiness_zone_min 4 driven by creeping thyme + USU. Source IDs reuse generic catalog institution IDs (celery pattern), each anchored to the specific thyme page actually read.

3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Annual or container. Zone 3 is below thyme's reliable in-ground hardiness, so it is grown as a single-season plant or, better, in a container moved to a sheltered, unheated spot for winter and brought back out after frost. Set nursery plants out promptly after the last spring frost to get a good first-season harvest before fall frost.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Thyme usually will not survive a zone 3 winter outdoors, so grow it for the season or keep it in a pot you bring somewhere sheltered for the cold months. Plant it after your last spring frost.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too cold to overwinter reliably in the ground here, so grow thyme as an annual or in a container you move under cover for winter. Set plants out only after the last spring frost; the season ends at the first fall frost.

4.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial, at the cold edge of reliable in-ground culture. Common thyme is rated hardy to about zone 5, but hardy selections (German Winter thyme, creeping thyme) and sharp drainage let thyme overwinter into zone 4; a sheltered, south-facing, very well-drained site helps. Treat it as a marginal perennial here, and keep a container backup where winters are severe.

Pick a hardy type like German Winter or creeping thyme, give it a sunny, very well-drained, sheltered spot, and it can come back each year. Keep a potted plant as backup for hard winters.

Sharp drainage and a sheltered spot, not the cold alone, are what carry thyme through winter here; wet frozen soil is the real risk.

description_seasoned: Thyme is a low, woody Mediterranean perennial in the mint family, grown for its tiny aromatic leaves that flavor soups, stews, sauces, meats, and fish. It forms a low, spreading, mat-like mound only about 6 to 12 inches tall and thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil; wet, rich soil rots it and dulls its flavor. Frequent harvesting and a light shear after its summer bloom keep it bushy, though it goes woody with age and is best divided or replaced every few years. It is hardy and pest-resistant, and its small pink, lavender, or white flowers are a strong bee draw.
description_beginner: Thyme is a low, spreading herb with tiny fragrant leaves you cook with. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it actually does worse if you pamper it. It grows only about 6 to 12 inches tall and spreads into a low mat. Snip it often and give it a light trim after it flowers to keep it bushy; it gets woody as it ages, so replace or divide it every few years. It is tough and rarely bothered by pests, and bees love its little flowers.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest thyme sprigs anytime once the plant is established: snip the top few inches of leafy growth, taking no more than about a third of the plant at once. Flavor is most concentrated just before and as the plant flowers, so cut for drying then, on a dry morning after the dew has lifted. Regular harvesting also keeps the plant from going woody.
harvest_ready_beginner: You can snip thyme anytime once it is established: cut the top few inches of leafy stems, taking no more than about a third at once. The flavor is strongest just before and as it flowers, so that is the best time to cut thyme to dry. Cut in the morning after the dew dries. Snipping it often also keeps it from getting woody.
hardiness_notes_seasoned: Thyme is a hardy perennial. Common, English, French, German Winter, and lemon thymes are reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9, and creeping thyme is hardier still, to about zone 4. With sharp drainage and a sheltered spot, hardy types push into zone 4, while zone 3 usually calls for growing thyme as an annual or a bring-in container plant. Good drainage matters as much as cold: thyme rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it, and it also struggles in hot, humid climates.
hardiness_notes_beginner: Thyme is tough and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 for the hardiest types like creeping and German Winter thyme if drainage is good). In the very coldest areas (zone 3), grow it for one season or in a pot you bring inside. Just as important as cold: thyme hates wet feet and will rot in soggy soil, and it also struggles in hot, humid places.
year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on root establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper off, and harvest only lightly. Thyme grows slowly the first season and reaches full size by about the second year, after which it produces steadily for several years before it should be divided or replaced.
year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the roots going. Water it fairly regularly until it is established, then cut back, and only pick a little. Thyme grows slowly at first and fills out by about year two, then produces well for several years before you replace or divide it.
soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Work only a little coarse compost into lean soil, and on heavy clay improve drainage with a raised bed or mound rather than digging in sand, which can worsen clay. Aim for lean, gritty, neutral to slightly alkaline ground; thyme does not want rich soil.
soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. Mix only a little coarse compost into the soil. If your ground is heavy clay, plant thyme in a raised bed or mound instead, because that drains better. The goal is poor, gritty soil, not rich soil.
bloom_time_beginner: Thyme flowers in summer, with tiny lavender, pink, or white flowers that bees love. The flavor is strongest just before it blooms. When yours flowers depends on where you live.
bloom_time_seasoned: Thyme blooms in early to mid summer, carrying small clusters of lavender, pink, or white flowers that are a strong pollinator draw. Leaf flavor peaks just before and as the flowers open. Exact timing shifts with your region and is set per zone.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, thyme slows or goes semi-dormant. Hold off on watering and feeding, leave any hard shaping for spring, and protect less hardy types or move container plants under cover. A resting plant needs almost no water, and it is wet soil or a late-fall hard cut, not the cold itself, that most often kills thyme over winter.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Where winters freeze, thyme mostly rests through the cold months. Stop watering and feeding it, save any big trim for spring, and in cold areas shelter the less hardy types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. A resting plant barely needs water, and it is usually soggy soil or a late-fall haircut, not the cold, that kills thyme over winter.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Thyme is grown for its leaves, not for fruit, so no cross-pollination planning is needed and a single plant is fine. Its small summer flowers are self-fertile and are a strong draw for bees, butterflies, and small beneficial insects, a bonus for the garden rather than something the plant needs.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one thyme plant, and you do not need a partner plant, because thyme is grown for its leaves rather than fruit. Bees and butterflies love its little flowers, but that is a bonus for your garden, not something the plant needs.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: After the summer flowers fade, shear off the spent flower stems and lightly reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth only and never into the bare woody base, which resprouts poorly. Frequent harvesting through the season plus this post-bloom shear keeps thyme compact; even so, plants go woody with age and are best divided or replaced every few years.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Once the summer flowers fade, trim off the old flower stems and neaten the plant, cutting only into the leafy parts and not into the hard woody stems, which do not grow back well. Snipping thyme often plus this trim keeps it bushy, but it still gets woody with age, so replace or divide it every few years.
